opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to frame it is that training is a capital expense and inference is an operating expense, and the two behave very differently as a business.

Training is a big, lumpy, upfront bet. You spend a lot on compute, data, and people to produce one model, and that model starts depreciating almost immediately, because six months later someone, maybe you, releases something better or cheaper. So training only makes economic sense if you can amortize it over a lot of usage. Training a frontier model is less like building a factory and more like making a blockbuster movie: high fixed cost, and the return depends entirely on how many people end up watching it.

Inference is where the money is actually made or lost. Every query costs real GPU time, so you have a marginal cost that doesn't really exist in traditional software. In the classic SaaS world, serving one more user is nearly free, so gross margins are 80 percent or more. With AI applications, if you're not careful, your gross margin can look more like a hardware or services business. That's a big shift for founders and investors who grew up with the old software playbook.

So over time I expect the balance to tilt heavily toward inference. Only a handful of companies will train the largest foundation models, but almost everyone will run inference, at enormous scale. Once a model is deployed widely, total inference spend over its lifetime can easily exceed what it cost to train. That's why I think a lot of the real engineering value is in the inference stack: better utilization of GPUs, batching, quantization, smarter scheduling, routing requests to the right-sized model, and making it easier to run open-source models efficiently. If you can cut inference cost by a few times, you change which applications are economically viable.

There's also a nice dynamic there. As inference gets cheaper, usage grows faster than the cost falls, a bit like Jevons paradox. Lower prices unlock new use cases, like agents that make dozens of model calls per task, which would have been unaffordable a year or two ago. So I'm less worried that cheaper inference shrinks the market. I think it expands it.

My practical advice for companies: unless training your own large model is truly your core differentiation, don't start there. Start from a strong existing model, fine-tune or adapt it, and put your engineering effort into serving it efficiently and building a great product. The winners won't necessarily have the biggest training run. They'll be the ones whose unit economics actually work when millions of people use the product every day.

r001.rationale: The response says each query incurs GPU cost and that lifetime inference spend can exceed training cost, but it does not clearly state that inference costs grow approximately linearly with application usage.

r002.rationale: It connects inference costs to gross margins and says engineering that lowers inference costs can make applications economically viable, framing the goal as workable unit economics at scale.

r003.rationale: It calls training a large upfront bet and says its economics depend on amortizing the cost across usage, with returns depending on how many people use the resulting model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that training and inference are really two different kinds of businesses, even though they share the same hardware.

Training is a capital expenditure. You spend a large, lumpy amount of money up front, you get a model artifact at the end, and then that artifact depreciates very quickly because someone will release a better one in six to twelve months. So the economics of training look a lot like R&D: you're betting that the model will be good enough, for long enough, to generate returns before it becomes obsolete. That's why only a handful of players can really afford to be at the frontier of pretraining. It's not just that the GPUs are expensive, it's that the payback window is short and uncertain.

Inference is the opposite. It's an operating expense that scales with usage. Every token you serve costs you something, and that cost compounds over the lifetime of the product. When I was at Alibaba and later building Lepton, what became very clear is that for any application that actually gets adoption, inference spend overtakes training spend surprisingly fast. You might train a model once for tens of millions of dollars, but if you have millions of users hitting it every day, you'll burn through that same amount in inference within months.

So the strategic question for most companies is not "how do I train a better model," it's "how do I serve a good-enough model as cheaply as possible." And that's where a lot of the engineering leverage sits: quantization, batching, speculative decoding, better kernels, smarter routing between large and small models. A two-x improvement in inference efficiency is worth far more to most businesses than a marginal improvement in benchmark scores, because it directly changes your gross margin.

There's also an interesting feedback loop. Cheaper inference lets you deploy more broadly, more deployment generates more data and more revenue, and that revenue is what funds the next round of training. So the companies that win long term are the ones who treat inference not as an afterthought but as the core of the business model, with training as the periodic investment that keeps the product competitive.

The last thing I'd say is that the open-source ecosystem has really changed this calculus. If a strong open model exists, the training cost for most companies effectively goes to zero, and they can put all their energy into inference and application. That's a healthy dynamic. It means the industry doesn't need everyone to spend a billion dollars on pretraining. A few do, and everyone else focuses on making that intelligence useful and affordable.

r001.rationale: It says inference spending scales with usage and that each served token has a cost, communicating that costs rise roughly in proportion to application usage.

r002.rationale: It says inference efficiency directly affects gross margin, but does not frame cost management as ensuring a sufficient profit margin from application usage.

r003.rationale: It describes training as a bet that the model will remain useful long enough to generate returns before becoming obsolete, linking the expenditure to future commercial returns.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the upfront investment from the ongoing cost of serving users. Training is a large, concentrated expense: you spend money to create a model before you know exactly how much demand it will have. Inference is a cost you incur every time somebody uses it.

So which one matters more depends on the scale of the business. If you’re experimenting with models and you don’t have many users yet, training may dominate your spending. But if you have a popular product, you keep paying for inference, and over time that can become the larger expense. A model that’s cheaper to train isn’t necessarily cheaper to operate.

The interesting question is whether spending more on training lets you reduce the cost of each useful response. Perhaps you can train a smaller model that performs a particular task well enough. If you serve that task millions of times, the inference savings can justify the additional training investment.

And I would measure cost per successfully completed task, rather than just cost per token. A cheap response that requires several retries may be more expensive than a slightly more costly response that gets the job done. Ultimately, the economics depend on what customers are willing to pay for that result and how efficiently you can deliver it.

r001.rationale: It says inference is paid for every use and can become the larger expense as a product grows popular, conveying that costs scale with application usage.

r002.rationale: It discusses what customers will pay and efficient delivery, but does not frame inference cost management as maintaining a sufficient profit margin on usage.

r003.rationale: It describes training as an upfront expense incurred before demand is known, but does not characterize it as a bet on the future commercial success of applications using the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the upfront investment from the ongoing cost of serving users. Training is a large, concentrated expense: you spend the money to create a model, and then you can use that model many times. Inference is a cost you pay every time somebody uses the product. If the product becomes successful, the cumulative inference cost can become much larger than the training cost.

So the business question is not simply, “How expensive is this model to train?” It’s, “How much value can I deliver per dollar of inference?” A more expensive training run might be worthwhile if it produces a smaller, more efficient model that can serve the same workload at lower cost. Conversely, a model that is cheap to train may still be expensive to operate.

There’s also a utilization issue. Training is generally a workload you can plan and run across a large cluster. Inference has to respond to user demand, often with tight latency requirements, so keeping the hardware efficiently utilized can be harder.

For me, the right way to look at it is over the lifetime of the product: training, inference, and the revenue or value those requests generate. You want the model that makes those economics work for your application.

r001.rationale: It says inference is paid for every use and cumulative inference costs can grow as the product succeeds, communicating growth with application usage.

r002.rationale: It discusses value per dollar of inference and lifetime economics, but does not frame cost management as ensuring a sufficient profit margin on application usage.

r003.rationale: It describes training as an upfront cost whose model can be reused, but does not characterize that expenditure as a bet on future commercial success.
